mechanism: The 3-token opening cue sets the base's deliberative register only through attention to the start of the answer, and that attention weakens as the answer grows. Past about 8,000 tokens the cued base slides back into pretraining-style continuation: fewer first-person deliberation words, and more textbook-style 'Problem/Solution/Exercise' blocks and restarted derivations. Its long hard328 answers are therefore lost to register decay, not to loops. RL writes the register into its weights, so it does not decay.
starts_from: [part: sampling/length] result-2c2cae (140 cued-base hard328 answers over 12,000 tokens, 11 right), result-51fd20 (forcing a commit on them loses problems; cap hits are failures to solve, not to stop), knowledge-787e53 (rule-A loops 0 at T 1.0), knowledge-1497e8 (the base finishes far more often from an RL prefix, which is dense in register). Observation built to explain: at T 1.0 the cued base's long answers fail without looping, and no stopping rule rescues them.
differs_from: all-1 (diffuse self-conditioning decay, refuted when half the RL delta gave +42 right with only 5 fewer cap hits). This one names one specific variable: register markers decaying with distance from the cue. It predicts that a re-inserted cue would restore the register, and it says nothing about delta scale. r4-m01 (self-similarity/zlib feedback): that predicts more compressible long texts, while this predicts less deliberative text that is not more compressible. m08 concerns base answers that are too short, not too long.
first_test: Files: hard328 e72c (base cue) and 86ef (RL plain) answers.jsonl. Keep rows with n_generated >= 12,000, cap hits included. Cut each text into 10 equal character deciles. In each decile compute F = matches of (?<![A-Za-z])(I|I'm|I'll|me|Let me|Okay|Wait|Hmm)(?![A-Za-z]) per 1,000 characters, and P = 1 if some line, after lstrip(), starts with 'Problem', 'Exercise', 'Question', '## ' or 'Solution:'. Statistic 1: median over rows of F(decile 10) / F(decile 1), per model. Prediction: base <= 0.5 and RL >= 0.8. Statistic 2: share of rows with P = 1 in deciles 8-10. Prediction: base >= 0.25, RL <= 0.05. Refuted if the base ratio is > 0.7, or if it is within 0.15 of RL's.

mechanism: For the cued base, T 0.6 and T 1.0 fail on different problems for different reasons. At T 0.6 the losses are loops on long problems. At T 1.0 the losses are tail-token slips on short, low-entropy problems that T 0.6 finishes cleanly. So the base's per-problem difficulty depends on temperature, and a second item axis appears between temperatures even though there is only one axis across T 1.0 arms.
starts_from: [part: sampling] knowledge-13cff3 (on the 402 problems that finish at T 0.6, T 0.6 gets 378 right against 361-364 for T 1.0), knowledge-9e4147 (plain base loses 28 points on short problems at T 1.0 but holds on the longest), result-5da8a9 (one axis across T 1.0 arms; T 0.6 cells not included). Observation built to explain: T 0.6 is more accurate than T 1.0 on the problems it finishes.
differs_from: r3-revise-2 says the T >= 1 failure set is a fixed set of long problems nested in the T 0.6 set, which predicts no T 0.6-only solves. r3-surprises-1 (tail slips everywhere, net zero from any tail cut) makes no prediction about which problems. r2-surprises-1/r2-all-2 put both temperatures on one surprise axis per problem. This one predicts problem sets that cross over, and puts the T 0.6-only solves on short problems. m07 is about wrong answers that repeat across prompts, not about sets that swap between temperatures.
first_test: Files: s3 r3/base-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (cue, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95; v3 recomputed from text with grader/rln4_grader_v3.py), day1_3/math500_base_cue-01/rows.jsonl (attempt 0, samples 0-3, score_v3), t1_t2_items per_problem.json (t2_generated_tokens). A = number of problems right in F_math500 (first row per problem) and wrong in all 4 T 1.0 samples. Prediction: A >= 10, with at least half in the lower half of problems by RL length. A one-axis/nested reading expects A <= 4: the base has 33 problems at 0/4, and T 0.6 is 56 problems weaker. Refuted if A <= 5, or if fewer than 40 % of the A problems fall in the shorter RL-length half.

mechanism: The RL-Math delta splits its function by rank. The top 8 singular directions per matrix carry a commit-and-stop policy: they box an answer and halt, cut cap hits, and do nothing about accuracy. The high-rank bulk carries the per-step error reduction: fewer slips and misreads, but no stopping. So top-8 alone makes quick wrong answers, while the bulk alone makes almost none but runs long and hits the cap.
starts_from: [part: weight differences] result-284db5 (hard328: top-8 cuts cap hits 77 -> 46, but RL minus top-8 hits the cap 90 times, more than the base, while still scoring 190), facts r5-m03 (full-500 top8 plain has 22 quick finished-wrong answers against the cued base's 13), result-d2933e (bulk 91 of 100). Observation built to explain: removing 8 directions raises cap hits above the base while accuracy stays near RL's, which no graveyard theory explained.
differs_from: r1-surprises-2 (low rank is functional, the high-rank remainder is optimizer noise): this gives the bulk a separate function. r5-m03 (top-8 = the cue and nothing more): this says top-8 is stopping, not register, and makes a different prediction about the bulk. r2-revise-1/r2-across-2 (the function lies in the dense sign pattern, all parts proportional): those predict the bulk and top-8 behave alike in kind. m04 is about the Think-SFT interpolation path, not about splitting the RL delta by rank.
first_test: Files: wsp1/screen100 bulk_plain-01, bulk64_plain-01, top8_plain-01, rl_plain-01 and base_cue-01 per_problem.json (first 100 MATH-500). Per arm, count Q = rows with score_v3 == 0, cap_hit false and n_generated <= 2,000, and C = cap hits. Prediction: Q(bulk_plain) <= 1 while Q(top8_plain) >= 3, and C(bulk_plain) >= C(rl_plain) + 3. Refuted if Q(bulk) >= Q(top8), or if C(bulk) <= C(rl_plain).

mechanism: On the path from base to Think-SFT, the imitated long-trace length policy arrives at a small fraction of the delta, while the accuracy needs nearly all of it. Midway models therefore write teacher-length answers without the teacher's ability to close them, and they hit the 16k cap more often than either endpoint. This is unlike the RL delta, whose gain saturates by a = 0.25.
starts_from: [part: weight differences] result-d2933e (halfway base -> Think-SFT with the cue scores 88 of 100), result-36e8cd (Think-SFT's top-8 directions break the base), result-bf6124 (24 of Think-SFT's 46 MATH-500 errors are cap hits), knowledge-b8d41a (bytegraft SFT dose curve peaks below 1 and collapses through stopping changes). Observation built to explain: an SFT delta carries a large-energy length component that the RL delta lacks. No graveyard theory explained the Think-SFT dose results.
differs_from: r5-m04 (full Think-SFT cannot close long traces, so its errors are cap hits on the longest problems; refuted on counts): this is about intermediate doses, and it predicts a cap-hit bump that is not monotone. WiSE-FT (the import) predicts accuracy stays high along the whole path; this predicts a dip in finishing. r3-external-2 (ExPO overshoot of the RL delta) is about RL, not SFT. m03 splits the RL delta by rank; this one is about dose along an SFT delta.
first_test: Files: wsp1/screen100 base_cue-01, sft025_cue-01, sft05_cue-01, sft1_cue-01 per_problem.json (first 100 MATH-500, cue, T 1.0). Count cap hits C and median n_generated M per arm. Prediction: max(C(sft025_cue), C(sft05_cue)) >= max(C(base_cue), C(sft1_cue)) + 3, and M(sft05_cue) >= 0.9 * M(sft1_cue). Refuted if neither intermediate arm has more cap hits than the larger endpoint, or if M(sft05) is below 0.6 * M(sft1). Check the plain arms too (sft025_plain against base_plain and sft1_plain).

mechanism: RL's extra hold-on words ('Wait', 'Hmm') come from a timer, not an error detector. RL learned to raise the hold-on probability with the number of tokens written since the last stated numeric result. Its excess over the base is near zero right after a result and grows over long stretches with no result stated.
starts_from: [part: interpretability readouts] result-b4c576/result-d68d37 (J-lens: hold-on readout +1.08 to +1.66 points in RL, wrap-up -1.40), result-c4411d (hold-on rise after a wrong result is about equal in base and RL), result-855858 (markers do not separate right from wrong samples), facts r4-m06 (RL re-check rate after wrong vs right candidates, ratio 1.24). Observation built to explain: RL's hold-on excess is real and general, but it does not follow errors.
differs_from: r4-m06 (a constant hold-on bias at every position; no gain on 3 offline tests): this changes the mechanism to a bias that grows with distance from the last result, and the constant version predicts a flat ratio. r2-revise-2/r5-m05 (better detection / better revision after a hold-on): those tie the hold-on to correctness, while this ties it to elapsed tokens. m06 is about sampled-token probabilities, not hold-on timing.
first_test: Files: s3 T1.jsonl (base cue) and T2.jsonl (RL), rows with cap_hit false. In each text, delete commas between digits. A result position is the end of each match of '=\s*-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?' or of a closing brace of '\boxed{'. For every character position, d = characters since the last result position (from text start if none). Bins of d: [0,200), [200,600), [600,1500), [1500, inf). Per bin and model: exposure = characters with d in the bin; events = starts of (?<![A-Za-z])(Wait|Hmm)(?![A-Za-z]) with d in the bin; rate = events per 1,000 exposure characters. Ratio R_b = rate_RL / rate_base. Prediction: R(last bin) / R(first bin) >= 1.5. A constant bias gives about 1.0. Refuted if <= 1.1.

mechanism: The cued base's errors are confident ones. A wrong step is drawn from inside the head of its distribution, not from the tail. RL's gain comes from swapping which head token wins at a few positions, not from trimming low-probability tokens everywhere. So RL's sampled texts hold as many low-probability tokens per 1,000 as the base's, and the base's wrong answers hold no more of them than its right ones.
starts_from: [part: interpretability readouts] result-faf15a (the base's located wrong step has log-prob -0.53 per token against -0.63 for control text; W4 refuted), result-44b4df (no truncation rule helps at T 1.0), result-fdc8da (top-1 tokens differ at about 8 % of positions). Observation built to explain: truncation cannot remove the base's wrong steps, because those steps are not unlikely. No graveyard theory explained the W4 result.
differs_from: r3-surprises-1 (RL shrinks the tail at every position): that predicts RL has far fewer sampled tokens with p < 0.01, while this predicts about the same number. r3-all-2/r2-across-1 (RL collapses entropy at fork positions): those predict a lower low-probability rate in RL text. m05 concerns hold-on timing, not sampled-token probabilities.
first_test: Files: hard328 e72c (base cue) and 86ef (RL plain) answers.jsonl, fields n_tok_p_lt_1e2, n_generated, score_v3, cap_hit. Statistic 1: pooled sum(n_tok_p_lt_1e2) / sum(n_generated) * 1,000 per model, then RL / base. Prediction >= 0.9. Statistic 2: within base finished rows, cut by quartiles of n_generated; in each quartile take (rate of wrong rows) minus (rate of right rows) and average, weighted by count. Prediction <= 0. Refuted if RL / base < 0.75, or if statistic 2 is > +0.3 per 1,000 tokens.

mechanism: Some hard problems carry a base-specific misreading attractor: the base, whatever its prompt, consistently parses the statement into the same wrong problem and lands on the same wrong value. RL's lower misread rate removes these attractors. So the base's wrong answers repeat across its own prompt variants far more than they match RL's wrong answers.
starts_from: [part: item-level structure] result-e41d94 (8 more 0-of-4 problems than binomial for the base), result-faf15a (RL cuts misreads by 1.52 nats, the largest drop of any error label), result-afc423 (33 base problems at 0/4 against 0.5 under a binomial null), facts r4-m07 p5 (on hard328, base and RL share the same wrong answer in only 0.19 of cases). Observation built to explain: the base's 0/4 problems are lumpier than independent slips allow.
differs_from: Revision of r4-m07, which said attractors are inherited from shared pretraining and kept by RL. It was refuted when only 0.27 of RL's wrong answers equalled a base wrong answer and RL fixed 12 of 16 such problems. The change: the attractors belong to the base and RL removes them, which predicts high agreement between base prompts and low agreement between base and RL. m02 is about which problems are solved across temperatures, not about the identity of the wrong answers.
first_test: Files: hard328 e72c (base cue), 7ba0 (base plain), 86ef (RL plain) and wdiff328 34ad (theta 0.5, cue). For each pair X/Y take the problems where both rows are cap_hit false, score_v3 == 0 and have non-empty extracted_v3. S(X,Y) = share where the two extracted answers are equal under the grader v3 equivalence function. Prediction: S(e72c, 7ba0) >= 0.35, against S(e72c, 86ef) of about 0.19, and S(e72c, 34ad) <= 0.25. Refuted if S(e72c, 7ba0) <= 0.25, or if fewer than 15 problems qualify.

mechanism: The base settles on a length budget for each problem from the prompt alone, before it writes; the probe reads this difficulty at the last prompt token. It fails between problems when that budget is too small for the solution, writing a short, compressed answer where RL writes a long one. So, at matched RL length, the base's wrong problems are those where its own answer is much shorter than RL's, even though within one problem its wrong samples run longer than its right ones.
starts_from: [part: item-level structure] result-b30f15 (across problems the probe at the last prompt token predicts failure at AUROC 0.73-0.77; within a problem it is at chance), result-5e17a6 (median right-answer tokens: base 1,432, RL 3,014), facts r5-m02 (within a problem, wrong samples are longer: +0.19 log ratio). Observation built to explain: the base knows how hard a problem is before it writes. No graveyard theory used that observation.
differs_from: r5-m02 (premature short commitment within a problem; refuted because wrong samples were longer than their siblings): this is a between-problem statement, consistent with that refutation. m01 is about long answers decaying, and this is about answers too short for their problem. r3-all-1/r1-across-2 (a stopping or token-budget controller learned by RL) put the mechanism in RL, while this puts it in the base's prompt-level allocation.
first_test: File: t1_t2_items per_problem.json. Keep problems with t1_cap_hit false and t2_right true. r = ln(t1_generated_tokens / t2_generated_tokens). Within each quartile of t2_generated_tokens (ties by problem_index), compute median r over T1-wrong problems minus median r over T1-right problems. Prediction: negative in all 4 quartiles, with the count-weighted mean <= -0.4. Refuted if the difference is >= 0 in 2 or more quartiles. Repeat on hard328, e72c against 86ef n_generated (RL-right, base-finished).

mechanism: The 3.0 RL-Zero releases trained at 12k with truncated rollouts masked, so every rewarded rollout ended before about 12k tokens. They learned a commit-by-12k habit: on problems that need more tokens they finish anyway and guess, rather than continuing or hitting the cap. This explains why their long-problem deficits come with few cap hits.
starts_from: [part: RL releases and rewards] r5-m08 review (Code 3.0 is 11.25 problems below the base on the longest quartile, yet has only 5 cap hits, against 27 for the base), knowledge-8a31ad (3.0 vs 3.1: 12k vs 16k, truncations masked vs negative), result-edceef (Code 3.0 cue 411, no math gain). Observation built to explain: a deficit confined to long problems that is not made of cap hits, which the graveyard left unexplained.
differs_from: r5-m08 (Code 3.0 learned a runaway long-generation mode; refuted by its 5 cap hits): this reverses the direction, to early forced finishing. r3-external-1 (3.0 keeps the base's loop basins; refuted when Math 3.0 scored 448): this predicts few loops and few cap hits but guessed finishes. m10 is about the order of learning within the 3.1 run, not about the difference between releases.
first_test: Files: s3 r3/fr-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (Math 3.0 first release, cue, T 0.6) and r3/s2800-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (3.1, cue, T 0.6); v3 recomputed from text. Among finished rows (cap_hit false): share with n_new > 12,000, and v3 accuracy of finished rows with n_new in [8,000, 12,000]. Prediction: share(fr) <= share(s2800) / 3, and accuracy in the 8k-12k band at least 15 points lower for fr than for s2800. Refuted if share(fr) >= 0.6 * share(s2800), or if the band accuracy gap is < 5 points. Confound to record: fr was run with the 3.1 tokenizer and prompt.

mechanism: Within the 3.1 RL-Zero-Math run, the first 100 steps install the answer format (box, then stop) and the deliberative length. The lower per-step error rate arrives only later in training. So at step 100 the policy's finished answers are no more accurate than the cued base's, even though their format already matches RL's.
starts_from: [part: RL releases and rewards] result-32b7a8 (by step 100, 478 answers open with 'Okay' and finished answers are 2.25x the base's length, with no gain in sharpness), facts r5-m07 (step-100 'Answer:' share is only 0.045, so the format has already moved), knowledge-87618d (most of the activation divergence on math text comes after step 100). Observation built to explain: format moves at step 100, while the activation change and the error reduction come late.
differs_from: r5-m07 said that by step 100 only the opening changes and the base's 'Answer:' format remains; it was refuted at a share of 0.045. This keeps the measured format shift and adds a claim about when accuracy arrives. r4-m10 (early entropy collapse sharpens finished answers) predicts higher finished accuracy at step 100, which this denies. m09 compares releases, not training steps.
first_test: Files: s3 r3/s0400_s0100-01/out/s0100/P_math500.jsonl, s0400/P_math500.jsonl, r3/s2800-01/out/P_math500.jsonl, and r3/base-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (cued base); all T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, first row per problem, v3 recomputed from text. Finished accuracy = right / (cap_hit false). Prediction: acc(step 100) <= acc(cued base) + 1.5 points; acc(step 2,800) >= acc(cued base) + 2.5; step 400 lies between them. Also count quick finished-wrong answers (n_new <= 2,000): step 100 >= 0.7 times the cued base's count. Refuted if acc(step 100) >= acc(step 2,800) - 1.

mechanism: The prompt asks for an 'Answer:' line, so the cued base sometimes commits answer-first: it writes the answer line early, then spends the rest of the text justifying that value instead of deriving it. This premature commitment, not slow reasoning, makes up much of its quick wrong answers. RL boxes only at the end.
starts_from: [part: grader and format] result-5e17a6 (13 wrong among the base's 263 answers of <= 2,000 tokens; RL 0 wrong at <= 4,000), result-fdc8da (the log-prob gap at the answer start follows the format), facts r4-m11 (the first marker is never right when the last is wrong, so the base does not overwrite a right answer). Observation built to explain: the base's short wrong answers are confident and never revised.
differs_from: r4-m11 (a right first answer later overwritten): this predicts the early first answer is itself wrong and kept. r5-m02 (short premature stops within a problem) used stopping length, while this uses where the first marker sits. m12 separates errors by marker type, and this by marker position; a cross-tabulation separates the two.
first_test: File: s3 T1.jsonl (base cue), rows with cap_hit false, v3 recomputed from text. First marker = the earliest 'Answer:' line start or '\boxed{' (as in the r4-m11 recipe). f = start position of the first marker / len(text). Early group: f < 0.5 and more than 300 characters after the marker. Late group: all other rows with a marker. Prediction: wrong rate(early) >= 2 x wrong rate(late), and in T2 the early group is < 5 % of finished rows. Refuted if the ratio is <= 1.3, or if the early group has fewer than 15 rows.

mechanism: The marker the cued base uses to state its answer shows which register produced the answer. An 'Answer:' line means the base is following the instruction in its deliberative register. A '\boxed{}' means it slipped into copying a textbook solution, which carries more slips and misreads. So at matched difficulty the base's boxed answers are less accurate than its 'Answer:' answers, and part of the cue-to-RL gap is the boxed-register share.
starts_from: [part: grader and format] result-fdc8da ('Answer:' line answers: 121 of 132 right; 338 answers boxed), knowledge-499152 (the base ends with an 'Answer:' line in 39-46 % of answers; RL always boxes), result-0018d3 (v3 gains for the base are format). Observation built to explain: the base's 'Answer:' answers are about 92 % right. No graveyard theory used the base's own choice of marker.
differs_from: r4-m11/r4-m12 (grader misses on overwritten or non-canonical answers; both refuted): this is not a grading error. It claims the marker type predicts true correctness. m11 is about where the marker sits, not its type. r1-all-2 (an answer-mode switch in RL) is about RL's format, while this is a within-base register readout.
first_test: Files: s3 T1.jsonl (base cue) joined with t1_t2_items per_problem.json (t1_right, t2_generated_tokens). Finished rows only. Type = 'answer' if the last answer marker is a line starting with 'Answer:', 'boxed' if it is '\boxed{'. Within quartiles of t2_generated_tokens, compute accuracy(answer) minus accuracy(boxed) and pool with count weights. Prediction: >= +5 points. Repeat on hard328 e72c using its mode_v3 field: >= +5 there too. Refuted if the pooled MATH-500 difference is <= +1 point or negative.
